Problems
========
1.  Plain-text password handling  
    • The function assumes that the value in stored is the real, un-hashed password.  
    • If the credential store or process memory is leaked, every user password is exposed.

2.  No salt or work factor  
    • Even if you intend to store a hash, the code gives no place to keep the salt or to apply a slow / memory-hard algorithm (bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt, PBKDF2).  
    • Fast unsalted hashes (MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256) make offline cracking trivial.

3.  Timing-side-channel leak  
    • The equality operator (==) returns as soon as it finds the first mismatching byte/character.  
    • An attacker who can measure response times can learn the password one character at a time.

4.  Type-safety / spoofing issue  
    • provided can be any Python object.  If it implements a malicious __eq__, that method runs inside your authentication code.  
    • A str/bytes cast guarantees you compare only primitive data and not attacker-controlled objects.

5.  Missing error handling / logging  
    • The function silently returns True/False.  In real code you usually want to distinguish between “user not found”, “wrong password”, and internal errors, and rate-limit repeated failures.

Fixes
=====

1.  Always store salted, slow hashes – never the raw password.

    import bcrypt      # or argon2, passlib, etc.

    def hash_password(password: str) -> bytes:
        # Generate a salt and hash in one step
        return bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode('utf-8'), bcrypt.gensalt())

2.  Verify with the library’s constant-time compare.

    def verify_password(stored_hash: bytes, candidate: str) -> bool:
        try:
            # bcrypt.checkpw is already constant-time
            return bcrypt.checkpw(candidate.encode('utf-8'), stored_hash)
        except ValueError:
            # hash has wrong format
            return False

3.  If you really must compare two strings/bytes yourself, use secrets.compare_digest:

    import secrets

    def compare_digest_safe(a: str | bytes, b: str | bytes) -> bool:
        a = a.encode() if isinstance(a, str) else a
        b = b.encode() if isinstance(b, str) else b
        return secrets.compare_digest(a, b)

4.  Enforce type, length, and encoding explicitly:

    def _to_bytes(s: str | bytes) -> bytes:
        if isinstance(s, str):
            return s.encode('utf-8')
        if isinstance(s, bytes):
            return s
        raise TypeError('Password must be str or bytes')

5.  Rate-limit and log failures where the function is called rather than inside the comparator.

Complete replacement example
----------------------------

import bcrypt
import secrets
import time

MAX_ATTEMPTS_PER_MIN = 5
failure_log: dict[str, list[float]] = {}

def _too_many_failures(user: str) -> bool:
    now = time.time()
    failure_log.setdefault(user, [])
    # keep only last minute
    failure_log[user] = [t for t in failure_log[user] if now - t < 60]
    return len(failure_log[user]) >= MAX_ATTEMPTS_PER_MIN

def verify_user_password(username: str, stored_hash: bytes, candidate: str) -> bool:
    if _too_many_failures(username):
        return False                      # or raise an exception / sleep

    ok = bcrypt.checkpw(candidate.encode(), stored_hash)

    if not ok:
        failure_log.setdefault(username, []).append(time.time())
        # extra constant-time step to equalize runtime for wrong password
        secrets.compare_digest(stored_hash, stored_hash)

    return ok

Key take-aways
==============

• Never compare raw passwords directly.  
• Store passwords as salted, slow hashes.  
• Use constant-time comparison (secrets.compare_digest or the library’s built-in).  
• Cast inputs to primitive types to avoid malicious __eq__.  
• Add logging/rate-limiting where authentication is performed.
